Checking and simplifying trigonometric identities

A trigonometric identity is an equation that is true for every angle where both sides are defined, such as sin⁡2x+cos⁡2x=1. This tool helps in two ways: it rewrites expressions in terms of sin⁡x and cos⁡x — the usual first step of a proof — and it tests the equation at dozens of angles. If any angle fails, you get a counterexample, which proves the equation is not an identity. In simplify mode, the expression is compared against a list of common simple forms.

Try changing the input

Check sin⁡2x=2sin⁡x (false) and then sin⁡2x=2sin⁡xcos⁡x (true). The graph shows the two curves separating or lying exactly on top of each other.

Supported identities

TypeIdentities
Reciprocalsec⁡x=1cos⁡x, csc⁡x=1sin⁡x, cot⁡x=1tan⁡x
Quotienttan⁡x=sin⁡xcos⁡x, cot⁡x=cos⁡xsin⁡x
Pythagoreansin⁡2x+cos⁡2x=1, 1+tan⁡2x=sec⁡2x, 1+cot⁡2x=csc⁡2x
Double anglesin⁡2x=2sin⁡xcos⁡x, cos⁡2x=cos⁡2x−sin⁡2x=1−2sin⁡2x

Expressions may use sin⁡,cos⁡,tan⁡,sec⁡,csc⁡,cot⁡, numbers, +,−,×,÷ and powers, with x as the angle.

Worked example

Simplify 1−cos⁡2xsin⁡x

Step 1 — Pythagorean identity

1−cos⁡2x=sin⁡2x

Step 2 — Cancel

sin⁡2xsin⁡x=sin⁡x(sin⁡x≠0)

How reliable is it?

  • "Not an identity" is certain: the tool shows an angle where the two sides differ.
  • "Identity" means the sides agreed (to within 10−9 relative error) at about 60 angles spread over (−2π,2π). This is very strong evidence but not a written proof; use the table above to build one.
  • Simplification only recognises the common simple forms the tool tests against (such as 1, sin⁡x, sec⁡2x, sin⁡2x). If none matches, it says so instead of guessing.
  • Angles where an expression is undefined (for example tan⁡x at π2) are skipped.
